children: A federal judge late on Thursday paused a US Army plan to detonate 68 barrels of toxic lead azide in Iowa after a lawsuit was filed by environmental groups in an effort to stop it.

The detonation of the degraded lead azide, an explosive used in military munitions, was initially planned for Friday. The army had postponed it until November 23 after public outcry by residents and farmers near Middletown, about 160 miles (257.5 km) from Des Moines.

The 8th US Circuit Court of Appeals granted a temporary stay of the permit issued by the US Environmental Protection Agency until the court can rule on a request for an emergency stay by the Iowa Environmental Council and the Sierra Club's Iowa chapter. It was not immediately clear when the court would rule.

Earthjustice, a nonprofit environmental law organization suing on behalf of the groups, said in a statement that the detonations would release "a toxic plume of lead dust into the air that could travel 100 miles north of the site, depending on weather conditions."

In a statement on November 19, acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle said it had determined with the EPA that a controlled detonation to dispose of the degraded lead was the option that posed the lowest risk to the public in the immediate and surrounding area.
Lead exposure can cause serious health problems, particularly in children, including damage to the brain and nervous system.

Earlier in the week, the Iowa Department of Agriculture and Land Stewardship recommended that cattle farmers near the detonation site move their livestock, feed and equipment to alternate locations or indoors, acknowledging that in some places, this would not be feasible.
On Friday, Patrick Wall, a beef field specialist with Iowa State University, said questions remained about what the impact of the detonation would be on livestock in the area.
"There's no research I can grab that says this is how a cow ingests lead this way," said Wall.
He said farmers were moving hundreds of cattle by truck to other locations.
This is especially costly at a time of high diesel prices, said Wall, but with beef at record prices, "they're just not willing to risk it."
Federal judge stays permit allowing Army to detonate lead azide near Middletown, Iowa
Army had postponed detonation to November 23 from November 20 after public outcry
Iowa agriculture department urged nearby cattle farmers to move livestock, feed and equipment
